title: Research
text:
Through Dr. Jimmy Hu at  UCLA’s B.I.G. program, my research investigated how regenerative populations, dental epithelial stem cells in the labial cervical loop of the mouse incisor, function differently in spastin overexpression; an enzyme involved in microtubule dynamics, which severs the microtubules to reduce Amelogenin, E-Cadherin, and Sonic Hedgehog (Shh) expression, generating a mutant population of altered cell arrangement. The analysis of the mutants was an ideal playground to learn computational scRNA-sequencing skills. However, early on, the issue was tackling the statistical effects of a small spastin-overexpressing population. After attempting a myriad of methods, I pivoted to incorporate pseudobulk differential expression and ranked-gene scoring to stabilize variance and reduce bias from the small sample size. Interestingly, the spastin-overexpressed population appeared to be more prevalent in the differentiated ameloblasts despite having impaired proliferative populations, prompting yet another challenge.
This led me to conduct a CellChat and SCENIC workflow focusing on the interactions between these cell populations, and I found that proliferative populations retained high levels of T-box transcription factor 1 (TBX1). Additionally, other undifferentiated populations retained upregulated proliferation pathways. Although the technical outcome was not what was expected, the experience strengthened my scientific resilience and ability to pivot in the face of experimental failure. I hypothesize that Tbx1 and Mafb are essential transcription factors in cell differentiation of the labial cervical loop, and further study can illuminate pathways relevant to tissue repair and gene therapy, transforming abstract mechanisms I investigate into actionable science.

SHARMA: In Dr. Sharma’s plant genetics laboratory at Cal Poly Pomona, my project focused on Pre- and Post-Fertilization Molecular Dynamics in Aquilegia Carpel Development. As a research assistant, I adopted RNA sequencing and reference-based transcriptome analysis techniques to investigate this novel system representing an early-diverging eudicot, and provide a window into the origins of floral complexity. Through transcriptomic profiling and scanning electron microscopy, I investigated the ABCDE model; MADs-BOX genes that govern carpel and ovule development, tracing how shifts in gene networks may have driven the diversification of reproductive structures across angiosperms. Through DESeq2 and cluster analysis, we identified crucial candidate genes, such as C-class Aquilegia homolog AqAg1, that can be instrumental in the successful transition to reproductive organs, such as carpels, from three developmental stages and ovules from pre- and post-pollination.
Further, while writing the manuscript, the genes’ divergent regulation across lineages prompted new questions: Could understanding these networks reveal how cells coordinate to repair or reshape tissues in other organisms? However, Dr. Sharma’s influence taught me what extends beyond these questions, particularly through agricultural innovation to support marginalized communities. As genes such as C-class Aquilegia homolog AqAg1 can be instrumental in the successful transition to reproductive organs such as carpels, they can improve yield in the floricultural industry.  Moreover, drafting grant proposals and presenting posters to explain these concepts instilled in me fundamental skills in communicating my science to a wider audience. Resulting in my project being awarded the Agricultural Research Institute Fellowship Grant, Project Hatchery Grant, STARs Program researcher, and my work will contribute to a manuscript with me as a co-first author.
Leong: Inspired by my work in agriculture, I became fascinated with how the human-regulated environment influences pollinators, further diminishing yield and the groups that depend on them. I joined Dr. Joan Leong’s entomology lab at Cal Poly Pomona in my sophomore year to investigate how Xenoglossa, Peponapis squash bees interact with government-supported pesticides. In the lab, I collaborated with Emily Roman, a Master’s student, to design her experiment of recording the approach and visiting behaviors of bees to squash flowers. The results yield that pesticides approved by the USDA and FDA reduce squash bee activities relative to the interval of honey bees, which explains the neglect to differentiate the species of pollinators present in agriculture. The skills I gained from Dr. Leong’s lab allowed me to solve problems holistically and continue helping underprivileged communities, as we continue to help these farmers, preliminarily shifting their chemicals to those that acknowledge biodiversity and encourage yield.

Service
text:
AMERICAN RED CROSS
I served as a Mass Care Member with the American Red Cross during the Dillon wildfires in 2025, supporting community members who had lost their homes. In this role, I collaborated with organizations such as the Salvation Army and World Central Kitchen to assist with feeding operations, shelter coordination, and large-scale distribution of essential supplies. This experience strengthened my ability to communicate with compassion and work effectively in high-pressure environments while contributing to community recovery efforts.

title: Service
text:
SHEPHERD’S PANTRY
Shepherd’s Pantry is an organization that provides non-perishable food, clothing, and resource counseling support services to homeless and low-income families in times of crisis. My role involved inventory management through computer systems and contributing to social advocacy efforts with city councils and school districts. Through this experience, I had the opportunity to connect with individuals from diverse backgrounds and help promote their independence and well-being.

title: Service
text:
PRETE FELLOWSHIP
I joined the Prete Fellowship at Kellogg Elementary School, where I taught students from diverse backgrounds sustainable gardening skills to promote equitable access to food education. I also developed lesson plans designed to engage students in learning about food systems and environmental sustainability. This experience allowed me to support student learning through hands-on, community-centered education.

title: Leadership
text:
LEADERSHIP STORIES



SACNAS
Wanting to cultivate that same growth within my community, a few friends established a SACNAS chapter — the Society for the Advancement of Chicanos/Hispanics and Native Americans in Science. This nonprofit provides a platform for minority scientists to address systemic issues. We partnered with industries that offer research opportunities while professors led workshops and mentorship programs, where members earned over $1,500.





BIOLA
The Biology Learning Assistant Program is a faculty-supported initiative to strengthen foundational biological sciences at Cal Poly Pomona. I taught biostatistics, computational biology, and cell biology to hundreds of students, while helping evaluate and refine curriculum to improve accessibility between lab and lecture.





ASM
Through the Achieve Scholars Mentorship Program, I mentor undergraduates from underrepresented communities. I guide students from entering their first research experiences to presenting at conferences, while also developing and leading workshops such as Essay Building, Scholarships 101, and Resume Building.





ALMA
In the Aspire-Learn-Mentor-Achieve program, I provide mentorship and educational workshops focused on academic advancement, financial aid literacy, and post–high school planning. I also design lesson plans that help students from underserved communities build competitive college applications.





HATCHERY
Through Cal Poly Pomona’s Projects Hatchery, I developed my skills in innovation, and grant writing by turning research ideas into actionable proposals. The program supports students from all majors in building meaningful projects from conception to implementation, with guidance throughout each stage of development. Building on my previous success securing the Agricultural Research Institute Fellowship, the STARs Program award, and the Project Hatchery Grant, this experience further strengthened my ability to write competitive proposals and prepared me to apply to the UCD Graduate Research Mentorship.
